tagline.text: A small island off Mactan with shallow emerald water and a long sandbar

location.label: Location
location.text: Getafe, northern Bohol, in the Camotes Sea between Olango Island and Bohol

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Day trip (half a day to a full day)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,200–2,500 (per person, Mactan island-hopping package, entrance fee and cottage)

children.text: Pandanon Island is a small island under Getafe in northern Bohol, one to one and a half hours by boat from Mactan, Cebu. Its waist-deep, clear water and long white sandbar make it a popular island-hopping day trip.

Pandanon Island sits in the Camotes Sea between Olango Island and Bohol. Administratively it belongs to Barangay Pandanon in Getafe, Bohol, but geographically it is closer to Mactan in Cebu, so it often appears on island-hopping routes from Mactan. According to Wikipedia, its area is only about 0.07 square kilometers and its population was 2,306 in the 2024 census. It lies roughly 9 km northwest of Getafe's port and about 13 km southeast of Cordova, Cebu. The island is inside the Danajon Bank, known as the only double barrier reef in the Philippines.

The name "Pandanon" is said to come from the pandan grass that once covered the whole island. The Philippine Star reports that the larger pandan variety used today as a dessert flavoring also grew here. During World War II, people from Cebu, Bohol and Leyte are said to have evacuated to the island to avoid detection and stayed until liberation, according to the Philstar, though other sources do not confirm this account. Before the war few people knew of it, and it was called a "hidden paradise." Even today it is a modest fishing island without major development. Fishing is the traditional livelihood, tourism is now the major income source, and some residents sell handmade shell accessories.

The island's appeal is its shallow, walkable sea. According to an April 2026 guide on sugbo.ph, the water is usually about waist-deep even a few meters from shore, with a long white sandbar and clear emerald water stretching to the horizon. At low tide the sand emerges and gives a "floating beach" look. The calm water also suits families with children. The Philippine Star, however, says the shallows are not ideal for snorkeling or diving, so for marine life you should take a boat to a neighboring island.

Pandanon is not a famous beach resort but a place for a day picnic. There is hardly any lodging, electricity and commercial facilities are limited, and most visitors stay on Mactan in Cebu or mainland Bohol and come for the day. Facilities are described as basic bathrooms, cottages and small stalls, so bring food and drinking water and carry plenty of cash. Typhoon Rai (Odette) in December 2021 badly damaged the island, residents were moved out beforehand, and many families lost homes and fishing boats, so even if it looks restored now, remember how modest village life is here. On arrival you are often briefed on simple village rules, such as taking your trash back and staying out of coral areas, so please follow them.

The island's signature view. The sandbar stretches out as the water recedes, with shallow emerald water on both sides. It is the best spot for photos and strolls, and the colors are clearest when the sun is lower.
The water is described as staying waist-high a long way from shore, which is safe. It is good for walking with children, but tides and wind change daily, so ask your boat operator about the tide.
You can rent a bamboo or wooden cottage to rest in the shade. Rates are given as about
depending on size, but figures differ by source, so confirm locally.
People spend time with beach volleyball, Frisbee, skimboarding and sunset watching. Equipment rental may be available depending on the day, so bring your own if you need it.
In the shallows you can see starfish of various colors and sizes, sea urchins and shells. Do not touch coral or animals; look with your eyes only.
One of the most visible buildings on the island is a small chapel. Walk quietly and respect the villagers' daily life. You can also buy souvenirs from residents who sell shell crafts.

There are designated cooking areas for visitors who cook, and islanders can be asked to prepare meals using local produce and fresh catch from local fishermen. Check availability and price in advance.

Tours often pair Pandanon with snorkeling at marine sanctuaries such as Hilutungan Island. Coral and fish are said to be easier to see at the neighboring islands. Nalusuan Island nearby is described as a calm-water stop with resort-style rest areas.

From Talibon, one described route is to take a bus to Getafe and then find a boat at the port.
The island is small enough to cover on foot, so no transport is needed. The sandbar and beach are within walking distance.

November to May, when the sea is calm and the sky clear, is described as the best time to visit, and Bohol-side guides single out December to April in particular. Weekends in the dry-season peak can be crowded. To avoid midday sun and afternoon wind, arrive in the morning.
Weekdays are less crowded than weekends and holidays. In the rainy season, weather can delay or cancel departures, so check sea conditions before you leave.

There is practically no lodging on the island, only cottages and small stalls. Most people stay in Cebu (Mactan) or mainland Bohol and make a day trip. Mactan has plenty of resorts and hotels, which suits an early departure.

Most visitors bring their own food or eat the packed lunch included in their tour. The island has cooking areas, and islanders can prepare meals with local produce and fresh catch if asked. Check price and availability as soon as you arrive. Many places take cash only, and there is said to be no ATM.

Bathrooms and washing facilities on the island are known to be modest. If you need to change, bring a plastic bag, spare clothes and a towel. A packed lunch eaten in a cottage lets you rest in the shade. Residents sometimes sell drinks and snacks, but the choice is limited.
There is little shade, so bring sunscreen, a hat, a long-sleeve rash guard and plenty of water.
There is no ATM and many places do not accept electronic payment, so carry plenty of cash.
Bring your own snorkeling gear; rental may not be available.
Use a dry bag and keep track of your belongings when boarding and disembarking, as the landing can be busy.
Arriving early avoids midday sun and afternoon wind and gives better photos.
Take all your trash back, especially to protect the sandbar and shallow coral areas.
Walk quietly through residential areas and ask permission before taking photos.
When booking, compare whether the tour price includes the entrance fee, environmental fee and cottage.
Boats may be cancelled when the sea is rough, so leave a buffer if you have a flight to catch.
Fees and rules are set by the local government and differ by source, so confirm with your boat operator before you arrive.
Electricity and commercial facilities on the island are limited and you cannot count on medical care. Bring basic medicines.
Even in waist-deep water there are tides and currents, so keep an eye on children.
Do not step on coral or sandbar life, and do not take marine animals.
Typhoons can badly damage the island, so check forecasts during typhoon season.
